title: Chapter 74 — Trust: The Mechanics of Credibility
intro: Trust is not a feeling. It is a series of signals you send through warmth, competence, honesty, and consistency.

sections.title: Warmth Before Competence
sections.content:
Research on first impressions shows that people evaluate warmth before competence. They ask 'does this person care about me?' before they ask 'does this person know what they are talking about?'

That is why Steps 1 and 2 — Engagement and Rapport — come before everything else. If the customer does not feel that you care about their situation, your product knowledge is irrelevant. They will not trust your recommendation no matter how accurate it is.

Warmth does not mean being fake. It means being genuinely interested in helping.

sections.title: The Trust Bank
sections.content:
Think of trust as a bank account. Every honest answer, every accurate recommendation, every followed-through promise makes a deposit. Every guess, every exaggeration, every missed callback makes a withdrawal.

The balance in that account determines how much the customer trusts your recommendation when it is time to close.

You cannot make a large withdrawal — like pushing a product that does not fit — if the account is empty. But if you have made steady deposits throughout the 10 Steps, the customer gives you the benefit of the doubt.

sections.title: Verification Builds Trust
sections.content:
Saying 'let me verify that for you' is one of the most powerful trust-building phrases in sales. It tells the customer you care about accuracy more than speed. It tells them you are not willing to guess with their money.

Ironically, admitting you do not know something increases credibility rather than reducing it. Customers do not expect perfection. They expect honesty. Humility creates trust.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating trust-building, ask:

Does the salesperson lead with warmth — or jump straight to product knowledge?
Do they make consistent trust deposits throughout the 10 Steps?
Do they verify information rather than guessing?
Does the customer appear to trust their recommendation by the time the close arrives?
